citation: Flynn E; Schwartz G; Brooks S; Catalano J (2023): Trace Metal Uptake and Mercury Methylation by Sediments from a Stream in Tennessee. Trace Metal Dynamics and Limitations on Biogeochemical Cycling in Wetland Soils and Hyporheic Zones. Dataset. doi:10.15485/1909710

dataset.name: Trace Metal Uptake and Mercury Methylation by Sediments from a Stream in Tennessee
description: The formation and transport of methylmercury (MeHg), a neurotoxin, in aquatic environments is a global concern for human health as MeHg can bioaccumulate and biomagnify to high concentrations in aquatic food webs. MeHg is formed by conversion from inorganic mercury through microbial mediated methylation. Sulfate-reducing bacteria have been identified as the primary organisms responsible for MeHg production. Pure-culture studies suggest that low availability of cobalt and copper may inhibit mercury methylation, but whether such limitations occur in the environment is unclear. To explore the possible interaction between trace metal availability and mercury methylation, sediments from the East Fork Poplar Creek in Oak Ridge, Tennessee were sampled and then incubated in the presence and absence of added dissolved cobalt and copper. Three types of data are provided in this package. The first reports the uptake of dissolved cobalt and copper by these stream sediments on short time scales (24 hours) in the form of final dissolved and adsorbed concentrations. The second data component consists of a time series of dissolved concentrations and pH values for stream sediments incubated with artificial stream water containing different addition levels of dissolved cobalt or copper. The dissolved concentrations reported include total iron, manganese, sulfur, phosphorus, nickel, zinc and cobalt, dissolved concentrations of sulfate and orthophosphate, and the amount of cobalt or copper adsorbed by the sediment. The third data component reports data at 0 and 72 hours of incubation time for stream sediments to which cobalt was added. These data include concentrations of methylmercury with isotope labeling to enable determination of methylation and demethylation rates as well as dissolved concentrations of sulfate, phosphate, chloride, iron, cobalt, and organic carbon. All data are provided in text-based CSV format with header sections indicating the data contained in each file and the corresponding units. Note that "u" is used in place of Greek lower-case mu to indicate the micro prefix on units. A Table of Contents file (Data_package_TableofContents.txt) provides an index for the data contained in the individual files.

spatialCoverage.description: EFPC 5.4: Stream bed location in East Fork Poplar Creek (EFPC) located 5.4 km upstream of the mouth of the creek. EFPC is a fourth-order stream in the Valley and Ridge Province of the southern Appalachians in eastern Tennessee, USA. The creek has experienced historic mercury contamination from the nearby Y-12 National Security Complex located at the creek headwaters. Sediment samples were collected in October 2018 and October 2020 from this location.

measurementTechnique:
Soil and Surface Water Sampling
Samples were collected in October 2018 from the East Fork Poplar Creek in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, U.S.A. The sampling site is 5.4 km upstream from the mouth of the creek (35°57’57.89” N 84°21’32.81” W WGS 84). Sampling occurred along from the northwest bank more than 25 days after the last significant rain event (rain >12 mm). Surface water was collected prior to sediment coring in 1 L Nalgene bottles for use with the mercury methylation and demethylation microcosms (see step 3 below). Sediment samples were collected by hand-coring using acid-cleaned polycarbonate tubes which were capped and sealed in the field. Sediment cores were brought into an anaerobic chamber and homogenized by hand mixing in a large bowl. The site water was filtered using 0.45 µm filters and Resazurin was added to it before being brought into the anaerobic chamber as well. Additional sediment sampling occurred in November 2020 at the same location. The sediment was mixed in an anaerobic chamber, double sealed in Ziplock bags, and shipped on ice to Washington University in St. Louis. It was immediately transferred to an anaerobic chamber for use with the metal uptake and exploration of effects of addition of cobalt and copper on sediments (see step 2 and 4 below).

Metal Uptake
The addition of cobalt and copper to sediment slurries may bind to sediments and organic matter, thus making it not bioavailable. To determine the concentration added to the sediment slurries in the incubations study, preliminary metal uptake experiments were conducted to explore a range of initial concentrations were completed in an anaerobic chamber. For the uptake experiments 0.2 g of the wet sediments were reacted with 0-300 µM CoCl2 or CuCl2 in 10 mL artificial creek water at pH 7.6 for 24 hours. Triplicate samples were prepared with initial metal concentrations of 10, 100, and 200 µM. Mineral-free controls were also created to assess errors in the initial metal concentrations. Samples were prepared in 15 mL polypropylene centrifuge tube, wrapped in Al foil to prevent any photochemical reactions, and rotated end-over-end.
After 24 hours, the final pH was measured, the sample fluid was decanted and filtered using disposable 0.22 µm MCE syringe filters. The filtrate was acidified to 2% HNO3 (trace metal grade) and stored for analysis. Cobalt and copper concentrations in the samples, blanks, and triplicates were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectroscopy (ICP-MS) on a Thermo Scientific iCapQ and Perkin Elmer NexION 2000, respectively. Aqueous and adsorbed concentrations of cobalt and copper were fit using a Langmuir isotherm. The predicted amount of metal adsorbed was then scaled by the sediment concentration to determine the amount of metal adsorbed in µM. The adsorbed metal concentration was added to the final dissolved metal to reconstruct the total metal added to the system to predict the metal concentration needed to be added for the sediment slurries for optimal dissolved metal concentration.

Mercury Methylation and Demethylation microcosms
To explore the effects of cobalt on mercury methylation and demethylation, microcosm samples were conducted over 72 hours in the presence and absence of cobalt. Sediments and site water were collected on the same day as the microcosms started. Sediment slurries of 10 g (±0.5 g) wet sediments and 20 mL surface site water were prepared in serum bottles. Bottles were capped, shaken to mix, and left in the glovebox overnight to equilibrate.
A total of 54 sediment slurries were created for 3 treatments (methylation, demethylation, ancillary), 3 Co additions (0, 100, 1000 µM), and two time points (0 hr and 72 hr). Each condition was completed in triplicates. Ancillary samples were used to determine pH, anions, dissolved organic carbon, dissolved total Fe/Fe(II), dissolved sulfide, and dissolved cobalt concentrations.
Cobalt, 201Hg (for methylation), and Me202Hg (for demethylation) spikes were added to appropriate samples and time began. Time 0 hour samples were ended ~5 to 10 minutes after the addition of spikes. To end the reactions, 10 mL of 18% KBr/5% H2SO4 was add to the methylation and demethylation samples. An isotope dilution spike for MeHg analysis was also added. Me201Hg and Me202Hg concentrations and rates of methylation and demethylation were determined at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.
For ancillary samples, sediment slurry was transferred to test tubes and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 15 minutes. Subsamples were preserved for different analyses. Five mL of the filtrate was acidified to 2% HNO3 using trace metal grade HNO3 and used to determine dissolved cobalt concentrations on ICP-MS. Samples for dissolved sulfide and pH measurements were diluted 1:2 using sulfur antioxidant buffer and measured on ion selective electrode and a pH electrode, respectively.

Exploration of effects of addition of cobalt and copper on sediments
To explore the effect of cobalt and copper addition on stream sediments trace metals and nutrients, sediments were reacted with the metals for 4 to 8 weeks in an anaerobic chamber. Sediment slurries were prepared in 250 mL glass serum bottles using 20 g of the sediments and 200 mL of artificial creek water at pH 7.6. The slurries were crimped sealed, wrapped in Al foil, and allowed to equilibrate overnight in the anaerobic chamber. Cobalt chloride and copper chloride were added to slurries to achieve 4 µM and 40 µM cobalt addition and 100 µM and 300 µM copper addition. These concentrations were determined by the metal uptake experiments to be within the optimal dissolved metal concentrations for mercury methylation in pure cultures. Samples were crimped sealed and remained undisturbed in the anaerobic chamber between sampling time points.
An aliquot of the solution was sampled at 1 hour, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 10, 14, 28 days for metal and nutrient characterization. An additional sample at 56 days was collected for the copper systems. At each allotted time, 16 mL were filtered using 0.22 µm disposable MCE filters. A portion of the filtered samples were acidified to 2% HNO3 and analyzed for trace metals (Cu, Co, Zn, and Ni) using a Thermo Scientific iCapQ ICP-MS and total iron, manganese, sulfur, and phosphorus on a Thermo Scientific iCAP 7400 DUO inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES).
The unacidified portion was used to measure pH, sulfide, Fe(II), sulfate, and phosphate. Sulfide concentrations were determined using an ion selective electrode (Hanna Instruments). Samples and standards were diluted 1:2 using sulfide antioxidant buffer prior to measuring. Sulfide standards were made from 0.01 M sodium sulfide made fresh in the anaerobic chamber and stored in a crimped serum bottle. The Fe(II) concentrations were measured with colorimetric analysis using the Ferrozine method on a uv-vis instrument. Sulfate and phosphate were measured using a Thermo Scientific Dionex Integrion High Pressure Ion Chromotrograph (IC) using a conductivity detector. Concentrations were determined using a Dionex IonPac™ AS19 analytical column (4x250mm) and Dionex IonPac™ AS19 guard column (4x50 mm) set to 30 °C and a constant flow rate of 1 mL/min. The eluent was generated from a Dionex eluent generator cartridge (EGC 500 KOH) to 10 mM KOH for 10 minutes then gradually increased to 45 mM KOH over 15 minutes before holding steady for 5 minutes.
